The requirement of a common bond was thus meant to ensure that 
each credit union remains a cooperative institution that is economically 
stable and responsive to its members’ needs. As a principle of internal 
governance designed to secure the viability of individual credit unions in 
the interests of the membership, the common bond provision was in no way 
designed to impose a restriction on all credit unions in the interests of 
institutions that might one day become competitors. * * * That the common 
bond requirement would later come to be viewed by competitors as a useful 
tool for curbing a credit union’s membership should not affect the zone-of- 
interests inquiry. The pertinent question under the zone-of-interests test 
is whether Congress intended to protect certain interests through a 
particular provision, not whether, irrespective of congressional intent, a 
provision may have the effect of protecting those interests. * * *
No t e
Continuing the Permissive Approach. After Nat'l Credit Union, the 
Supreme Court has continued its relatively permissive approach toward the 
zone of interests test. In Thompson v. North American Stainless, LP, 562 U.S. 
170, (2011), the Court considered whether an employee’s Title VII claim 
against his employer for retaUation, alleging that his termination was 
motivated by a gender discrimination complaint filed with the EEOC by his 
fiancee who worked for the same employer, fell within that statute’s zone of 
interests. The employer argued that while Title VIFs anti-retaliation 
provisions certainly protected the fiancee, Thompson fell outside the statute’s 
zone of interests because he did not engage in any protected conduct and 
therefore was not the statute’s intended beneficiary. The Supreme Court, with 
Justice Scaha writing, disagreed, noting that “the purpose of Title VII is to 
protect employees from their employers’ unlawful actions.” Because Thompson 
was “not an accidental victim of the retahation—collateral damage, so to 
speak, of the employer’s unlawful act,” but rather was “the employer’s intended 
means of harming [Thompson’s fiancee],” the Court held he fell “well within 
the zone of interests sought to be protected by Title VII.”
Similarly, in Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians v. 
Patchak, 567 U.S. 209 (2012), the Court held that a property owner who filed 
suit challenging the Secretary of the Interior’s decision to acquire nearby land 
in trust for an Indian tribe seeking to open a casino was within the zone of 
interests of the Indian Reorganization Act. That Act permitted the Secretary 
to acquire property “for the purpose of providing land for Indians.” Although 
Patchak was not “an Indian or tribal official seeking land,” nor did he “claim 
an interest in advancing tribal development,” the Court held that his alleged 
economic, environmental, and aesthetic harm as a nearby property owner was 
Rufficient to bring him within the statute’s zone of interests. In so holding, the
